_description: VC2 Content Descriptions organised into thematic units of work
_note: English and Maths have native year levels (7-10). All other areas use curriculum bands (8=Years 7-8, 10=Years 9-10) with student-selected CDs.

contentDescriptions.description: We are learning how the language we use both expresses and creates our personal and social identities.
We are learning about the language of evaluation — how people express judgments — and substantiation — how they back up their claims with evidence.
We are learning to identify and describe how texts are structured differently depending on their purpose, and how language features vary across different types of texts.
We are learning how texts use devices like overviews, examples, illustrations and other structural signals to create cohesion and guide the reader through the content.
We are learning how complex and compound-complex sentences can be used to elaborate, extend and explain ideas in sophisticated ways.
We are learning how using consistent tense through verbs and verb groups keeps our writing clear and easy to follow.
We are learning how still images, moving images and sound can be used to create a particular perspective or point of view.
We are learning about the role vocabulary plays in building specialist knowledge, including understanding words that mean different things in everyday versus specialist contexts.
We are learning how to use colons and brackets to support and extend meaning in our writing.

We are learning to identify and explore ideas, points of view, characters, events and issues in stories from different historical, cultural and social contexts — including texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors.
We are learning to develop opinions about characters, settings and events in stories, identifying where we agree or disagree with other readers' interpretations.
We are learning how literary devices, language features, dialogue and visual elements are used to create meaning and emotion in literary texts.
We are learning to identify and explain how characters, settings and events work together to create meaning in literary texts.
We are learning to identify and explain how literary devices create layers of meaning and aesthetic qualities in texts — including in poetry.
We are learning to create our own texts that experiment with the literary language features and devices we have encountered in our reading.
We are learning to use interaction skills when discussing ideas and information, including when evaluating features of texts.
We are learning to deliver structured spoken texts for specific purposes and audiences, using formal language and effective vocal features.
We are learning to use spelling rules, word parts, patterns and word origins to spell accurately and independently — including when using a dictionary or digital tools.
We are learning to explain how current technology affects the way we read, create and respond to texts, including media texts.
We are learning to analyse how language features shape meaning and vary depending on the audience and purpose of a text.
We are learning to explain how ideas in texts are organised using structures like taxonomies, cause and effect, extended metaphors and chronological order.
We are learning to use comprehension strategies — including inferring — to build literal and inferred meaning from increasingly complex texts.
We are learning to create different types of texts — written and spoken — selecting subject matter, language and print features suited to our purpose.
We are learning to review and edit our own texts and others' by removing repetition, refining ideas, reordering sentences and adding or substituting words for impact.
We are learning how language actively shapes relationships and the roles people take on within those relationships.
We are learning how language features like simile and metaphor can add layers of meaning to evaluative and substantiating language.
We are learning how texts are structured according to their purpose, how language features vary, and that some texts combine features from multiple text types.
We are learning how cohesion in texts is improved by strengthening internal structures — using evidence, quotations and references to connect and support ideas.
We are learning to examine different clause structures — including embedded clauses — that add information and expand ideas in complex sentences.
We are learning how nominalisation — turning verbs or adjectives into nouns — changes the way information is presented in texts.
We are learning how still images, moving images and sound use intertextual references — connections to other texts — to enhance and layer meaning.
We are learning about the role of academic vocabulary — the formal, precise language used across disciplines — and how to use it effectively.
We are learning how to use semicolons and dashes to extend our ideas and support meaning in our writing.

We are learning to explain how ideas, issues and points of view in literary texts from diverse historical, cultural and social contexts — including by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors — reflect their context.
We are learning to explore and discuss opinions about the language features, literary devices and text structures that contribute to the styles of literary texts.
We are learning to explain how language and visual elements in a range of literary texts influence how audiences respond to and interpret characters, events, settings and themes.
We are learning to identify intertextual references in literary texts and explain how they create new layers of understanding.
We are learning how language features like sentence patterns create tone and voice, and how literary devices like imagery shape the reader's interpretation.
We are learning to create texts that experiment with literary language features and devices for particular purposes and effects.
We are learning to use interaction skills for specific purposes and contexts, including when supporting or challenging ideas and positions in discussions.
We are learning to deliver structured spoken texts for particular purposes and audiences, adjusting for formal and informal contexts and using effective vocal and visual features.
We are learning to use our knowledge of spelling patterns to spell technical and academic words consistently and accurately.
We are learning to describe how representations of people, places and events in texts reflect the context in which those texts were created.
We are learning to analyse and evaluate how language features represent perspectives on issues, events, situations, individuals or groups.
We are learning to analyse how authors organise ideas to develop and shape the meaning of their texts.
We are learning to use comprehension strategies — including inferring — to build both literal and inferred meaning from complex texts across subjects.
We are learning to create different types of texts — written and spoken — that raise issues, report events and advance opinions, using deliberate language choices.
We are learning to review and edit to refine and clarify ideas, improving the effectiveness and coherence of our own texts and others'.
We are learning how language strengthens relationships and the dynamics of roles within those relationships.
We are learning how evaluative and substantiating language expresses individual views and values through specific language features including modality.
We are learning how text structures and language features can be adapted and altered according to the purpose of a text.
We are learning how cohesive devices — including nominalisation — condense information and link, expand and elaborate on ideas across a text.
We are learning how authors vary sentence structures for effect — such as using sentence fragments, or deliberately placing dependent clauses in unusual positions.
We are learning how abstract nouns can be used to summarise and encapsulate complex ideas in a text.
We are learning to analyse how symbols in still and moving images and the use of sound augment and extend the meaning of a text.
We are learning to analyse how vocabulary choices contribute to the style, mood and tone of a text.
We are learning to use punctuation conventions for condensing information and for formal referencing and citation.

We are learning to analyse how people and places are represented in literary texts from diverse historical, cultural and social contexts — including texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors.
We are learning to explore and develop our personal responses to literary texts, comparing how our initial impressions change as we engage more deeply.
We are learning to analyse how literary devices, language features and visual elements shape an audience's preferences about the representation of characters, events, settings and themes.
We are learning to analyse the effect of text structures, language features and literary devices such as extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory and symbolism on the interpretation of literary texts.
We are learning to analyse how text structures, language features and literary devices in literary texts create aesthetic qualities that appeal to readers.
We are learning to create texts — which may blend genres — that experiment with literary structures, language features, devices and voice.
We are learning to use interaction skills to discuss opinions about texts with different purposes and audiences, analysing how language is used to influence.
We are learning to deliver structured spoken texts for particular purposes, demonstrating different levels of formality and using features of voice, visual elements and content selection effectively.
We are learning to spell accurately and consistently, and to understand that non-standard spelling can be used in texts deliberately for particular effects.
We are learning to analyse how representations of people, places, events and concepts in texts reflect the contexts in which those texts were created.
We are learning to analyse and evaluate how language features are used to explicitly represent values, beliefs and attitudes in texts.
We are learning to analyse the organisation of ideas in paragraphs and extended texts, and to evaluate the impact of that organisation on meaning.
We are learning to integrate comprehension strategies to build literal, inferred and evaluative meanings from complex and challenging texts.
We are learning to create different types of texts — written and spoken — that present a point of view, advance ideas, and use evidence and argument effectively.
We are learning to review and edit our own texts and others' to improve clarity, coherence and control over content, organisation, sentence structure, vocabulary and punctuation.
We are learning how language can have inclusive and exclusive social effects — how it can empower or disempower people and groups.
We are learning that evaluative and substantiating language — whether stated directly or implied — reveals an author's views and values.
We are learning to analyse text structures and language features and evaluate their effectiveness in achieving a text's purpose.
We are learning how authors select and vary text structures to create sequence and cohesion throughout a text.
We are learning to analyse and evaluate how specific sentence structures express and craft ideas with precision and effect.
We are learning to analyse how syntax — the arrangement of words and phrases — contributes to both meaning and style.
We are learning to evaluate how the features of still and moving images and the use of sound create effects and shape representations.
We are learning to understand and use an expanded vocabulary with precision — choosing exactly the right word for every context.
We are learning to use and experiment with punctuation for meaning and effect — going beyond correctness to use punctuation as a creative and rhetorical tool.

We are learning to analyse representations of individuals, groups and places in literary texts — including texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors — and evaluate how those representations reflect their context.
We are learning to synthesise our own interpretation of a literary text and explore how others interpret the same text differently.
We are learning to analyse how social, moral or ethical positions are represented across a range of literary texts.
We are learning to analyse how text structure, language features, literary devices and intertextual connections all work together to shape how we interpret literary texts.
We are learning to compare and evaluate how 'voice' as a literary device is used across different texts to evoke emotional responses and create aesthetic effects.
We are learning to create texts with a sustained voice, selecting and adapting literary structures, devices, language and audiovisual features for specific purposes and effects.
We are learning to use interaction skills to discuss opinions about texts, analysing the purposes and effects of text structures and language features in group discussions.
We are learning to deliver structured spoken texts for particular purposes, experimenting with formality and making deliberate decisions about how to engage our audience.
We are learning to use our full knowledge of the spelling system to spell accurately and to manipulate standard and non-standard spelling for particular effects.
We are learning to analyse and evaluate how representations of people, places, events and concepts in texts reflect the contexts in which they were created.
We are learning to analyse and evaluate how language features are used to both implicitly and explicitly represent values, beliefs and attitudes.
We are learning to analyse and evaluate how authors organise ideas in texts to achieve their purpose — examining the relationship between structure and meaning.
We are learning to integrate comprehension strategies seamlessly to build literal, inferred and evaluative meaning from the most complex and challenging texts.
We are learning to create different types of texts — written and spoken — that reflect on challenging and complex issues, combining different modes and using sophisticated language choices.
We are learning to review, edit and refine our own texts and others' for control and coherence of content, organisation, sentence structure, vocabulary and punctuation.
We are learning the relationship between perfect squares and square roots, and how to use them in calculations.
We are learning to write numbers in expanded notation using powers of 10, and as products of prime factors.
We are learning to find equivalent rational numbers and represent positive and negative fractions and decimals on number lines.
We are learning to round decimals appropriately and use estimation to check if our calculations are reasonable.
We are learning efficient strategies for multiplying and dividing fractions and decimals.
We are learning to use all four operations with positive rational numbers to solve problems.
We are learning to find percentages of quantities and express one quantity as a percentage of another.
We are learning to compare, order and perform addition and subtraction with integers (positive and negative numbers).
We are learning to recognise, represent and solve problems involving ratios.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems with rational numbers and percentages.
We are learning to use variables to represent formulas and substitute values to find unknowns.
We are learning to use algebraic laws (associative, commutative, distributive) to simplify expressions.
We are learning to solve linear equations with whole number solutions and verify answers by substitution.
We are learning to investigate relationships between variables shown in graphs based on real-world data.
We are learning to generate tables of values from patterns or rules and plot them on the Cartesian plane.
We are learning to manipulate formulas with several variables and explore what happens when variables change.
We are learning the formulas for areas of rectangles, triangles and parallelograms, and applying them to solve problems.
We are learning to calculate the volume of right prisms using formulas.
We are learning about the number π and its relationship to a circle's circumference, radius and diameter.
We are learning about angle relationships formed when parallel lines are crossed by a transversal.
We are learning that the angles inside a triangle always add up to 180°, and using this to solve problems.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling with ratios, percentages and proportional relationships to solve real-world problems.
We are learning to represent 3D objects in 2 dimensions and evaluate different representations.
We are learning to classify triangles and quadrilaterals by their side and angle properties.
We are learning to describe how translations, reflections and rotations change coordinates on the Cartesian plane.
We are learning to design algorithms that classify shapes based on their properties.
We are learning to identify sample spaces for experiments, assign probabilities and predict how many times an outcome might occur.
We are learning that running many trials produces results closer to expected probabilities, and we can use technology to simulate this.
We are learning to calculate the range, median, mean and mode for data sets and decide which measure best represents the data.
We are learning to create dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots, and describe distributions by shape, centre and spread.
We are learning to plan and conduct statistical investigations using data from primary and secondary sources.
We are learning to recognise irrational numbers like π and √2 in applied contexts, and understand they cannot be written as exact fractions.
We are learning the exponent laws for positive integer exponents and the zero exponent.
We are learning to convert between fractions and terminating or recurring decimals.
We are learning to perform all four operations with integers and rational numbers using efficient strategies.
We are learning to solve problems involving percentage increases, decreases and percentage of a quantity.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems with rational numbers and percentages.
We are learning to expand, factorise, rearrange and simplify linear expressions using algebraic properties.
We are learning to graph linear relations, solve linear equations and inequalities, and verify our solutions.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling with linear relations to solve applied problems.
We are learning to use algorithms and testing procedures to find and fix errors.
We are learning to experiment with linear functions using digital tools, making conjectures and verifying them.
We are learning to solve area and perimeter problems involving irregular and composite shapes.
We are learning to calculate the volume and capacity of right prisms.
We are learning to use formulas to find the circumference and area of circles.
We are learning to solve time problems including working across different time zones.
We are learning to use rates to compare quantities measured in different units.
We are learning to apply Pythagoras' theorem to find unknown sides of right-angled triangles.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving ratios, rates and proportions.
We are learning the conditions for triangles to be congruent or similar, and extending these ideas to quadrilaterals.
We are learning to establish properties of quadrilaterals using congruent triangles and angle relationships.
We are learning to describe 3D positions using a three-dimensional coordinate system.
We are learning to design and test algorithms that identify congruent or similar shapes.
We are learning that complementary events have probabilities that add to 1, and how to use this to solve problems.
We are learning to find all possible outcomes for two combined events using tables, tree diagrams and the fundamental counting principle.
We are learning to use repeated experiments and simulations to estimate probabilities for compound events.
We are learning the difference between a population and a sample, and comparing data collected from different sources.
We are learning to analyse data distributions from different sampling techniques.
We are learning that random samples from the same population can give different results, and exploring how sample size affects this variation.
We are learning to plan and conduct statistical investigations about a population using sampling methods.
We are learning that the real number system includes both rational and irrational numbers, and we can represent all real numbers on the number line.
We are learning to apply exponent laws to numerical expressions with integer exponents, including negative exponents.
We are learning to simplify, expand and factorise algebraic expressions including binomial products and common factors.
We are learning to sketch linear graphs in various forms and solve linear equations.
We are learning to find the gradient, midpoint and distance between two points on the Cartesian plane.
We are learning to identify, graph and solve quadratic functions and equations, including using the null factor law.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling with linear or quadratic functions to solve applied problems.
We are learning to explore how changing parameters in a function affects its graph.
We are learning to calculate the volume and surface area of prisms, cylinders and composite objects.
We are learning to work with very large and very small measurements expressed in scientific notation.
We are learning to solve spatial problems using angle properties, scale, similarity, Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry.
We are learning to calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors in measurements.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling with direct proportion, rates, ratio and scale to solve practical problems.
We are learning that the sine, cosine and tangent ratios stay constant for a given angle in right-angled triangles, and applying them to find unknown sides and angles.
We are learning to apply enlargement transformations and describe what changes and what stays the same.
We are learning to design, test and refine algorithms based on geometric constructions and theorems.
We are learning to list all outcomes for two-step experiments (with and without replacement) and assign probabilities.
We are learning to use relative frequencies to estimate probabilities involving 'and', 'or' and 'not'.
We are learning to design and run simulations to estimate probabilities that cannot be calculated easily.
We are learning to analyse survey reports from digital media to evaluate how data was collected and whether conclusions are valid.
We are learning how different sampling methods and sample selections can affect survey results and representativeness.
We are learning to represent and compare data distributions using back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots and histograms.
We are learning to choose the best type of display for our data and justify our choices.
We are learning to plan and conduct full statistical investigations, analyse the data and evaluate our conclusions.
We are learning to recognise how using approximate values in repeated calculations can cause errors to accumulate.
We are learning to factorise algebraic expressions by identifying and extracting a common algebraic factor.
We are learning to simplify algebraic products and quotients using the laws of exponents.
We are learning to add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic fractions with simple denominators.
We are learning to expand binomial products and factorise monic quadratic expressions using various methods.
We are learning to substitute values into formulas and rearrange formulas to solve for different variables.
We are learning to implement algorithms using data structures in pseudocode or a programming language.
We are learning to solve problems involving linear equations, including those derived from real-world situations and formulas.
We are learning to solve linear inequalities and represent their solutions on a number line.
We are learning to solve pairs of simultaneous linear equations using algebraic and graphical methods.
We are learning to solve problems involving the gradients of parallel and perpendicular lines.
We are learning to explore how algebraic and graphical representations connect for quadratic, reciprocal and other non-linear functions.
We are learning to solve linear equations that contain algebraic fractions.
We are learning to solve simple quadratic equations using strategies including the null factor law.
We are learning to solve simple exponential equations.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling with linear, quadratic and exponential functions to solve real-world problems.
We are learning to solve equations graphically or by systematic guess-check-and-refine, using digital tools.
We are learning about polynomials and how to apply the factor and remainder theorems.
We are learning to devise and use algorithms and simulations to solve mathematical problems.
We are learning to simplify combinations of linear expressions with rational coefficients and solve equations with algebraic fractions.
We are learning about the inverse relationship between exponential and logarithmic functions.
We are learning to describe, interpret and sketch parabolas, hyperbolas, circles and exponential functions from their equations.
We are learning to use polynomial understanding to sketch curves and describe their features from their equation.
We are learning to factorise both monic and non-monic quadratic expressions and solve a wide range of quadratic equations.
We are learning to use function notation like f(x) to describe relationships between dependent and independent variables.
We are learning to solve linear and non-linear simultaneous equations using graphing or systematic methods.
We are learning to experiment with functions and relations using digital tools, making conjectures and verifying them.
We are learning to define rational and irrational numbers, and perform operations with surds and fractional exponents.
We are learning to perform operations involving fractional exponents and surds.
We are learning to define logarithms, apply log laws and investigate logarithmic scales.
We are learning to solve problems involving the surface area and volume of composite 3D objects.
We are learning to interpret and use logarithmic scales in contexts involving very small or very large quantities.
We are learning to apply Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to solve practical problems, including in three dimensions.
We are learning to use mathematical modelling to solve problems involving direct and inverse proportion.
We are learning to solve problems involving the surface area and volume of pyramids, cones, spheres and composite objects.
We are learning to explore how the average rate of change approaches a limiting value as intervals become smaller.
We are learning to use deductive reasoning to write geometric proofs and apply theorems to solve spatial problems.
We are learning to interpret network diagrams that represent real-world relationships and describe their features.
We are learning to prove and apply angle relationships involving radii, diameters, chords and tangents of circles.
We are learning the sine rule, cosine rule and area rule for any triangle and applying them to problems.
We are learning to define sin(x), cos(x) and tan(x) using the unit circle and graph these trigonometric functions.
We are learning to solve simple trigonometric equations.
We are learning to apply Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to solve three-dimensional problems.
We are learning to design, test and refine algorithms for spatial problems, and communicate and justify our approaches.
We are learning to investigate conditional probability using language like 'if...then', 'given' and 'knowing that'.
We are learning to analyse multi-step chance experiments, assign probabilities and investigate the concept of independence.
We are learning about counting principles and factorial notation for efficient counting in probability and combinatorics.
We are learning to evaluate research studies reported in the media by examining their planning and implementation.
We are learning to use quartiles, interquartile range and boxplots to compare data distributions.
We are learning to construct scatterplots, fit a line of good fit and describe the association between two numerical variables.
We are learning to construct two-way tables and analyse possible relationships between categorical variables.
We are learning to critically analyse statistical claims in media by examining displays, statistics and sampling methods.
We are learning to plan and conduct bivariate statistical investigations, including time-series analysis.
We are learning to calculate and interpret mean and standard deviation, and use them to compare data sets.
We are learning about different measures of spread and how useful each one is for different distributions.
We are learning to investigate bivariate data using digital tools, fit a straight line, make predictions and assess the strength of association.
We are learning that scientific knowledge — including models and theories — can change when new evidence comes to light.
We are learning that advancing scientific knowledge involves people from different backgrounds, perspectives and worldviews working together.
We are learning that scientific responses to real-world issues can involve ethical, environmental, social and economic trade-offs.
We are learning that communicating scientific knowledge to the public plays an important role in shaping people's views and government policies.
We are learning to develop investigable questions, predictions and hypotheses that guide our investigations and help us identify patterns and test relationships.
We are learning to plan reproducible investigations by identifying variables, managing risks, considering ethical issues and following cultural protocols on Country.
We are learning to select appropriate equipment and use it to generate and record data with attention to precision.
We are learning to organise and process data by constructing appropriate representations such as tables, graphs, keys and models.
We are learning to analyse processed data to identify patterns, trends, relationships and anomalies.
We are learning to evaluate scientific methods and conclusions by identifying assumptions, sources of error, conflicting evidence and unanswered questions.
We are learning to construct evidence-based arguments to support conclusions or evaluate claims, including considering ethical issues when using secondary data.
We are learning to communicate scientific ideas, findings and arguments by choosing formats, vocabulary and representations suited to our purpose and audience.
We are learning that organisms can be classified into groups based on similarities and differences, and tools like dichotomous keys help us organise this diversity.
We are learning that cells are the basic building blocks of all life, and different types of cells have specialised structures that carry out specific functions.
We are learning that the structure of cells, tissues and organs is directly related to their function, and that organ systems keep organisms alive.
We are learning that matter and energy flow through ecosystems via food webs and food pyramids, and that changes to any part of the system can affect the whole ecosystem.
We are learning that the particle and kinetic theories explain how the arrangement and movement of particles determine a substance's properties and behaviour.
We are learning that matter can be classified as pure substances or mixtures, and mixtures can be separated using techniques based on their components' properties.
We are learning that atomic theory explains the difference between elements, compounds and mixtures, and that we represent them using symbols and chemical formulas.
We are learning to distinguish physical changes from chemical changes by looking for signs like colour change, gas production, temperature change or precipitate formation.
We are learning that Earth's resources can be renewable or non-renewable, and that how we extract and use them involves both benefits and risks to sustainability.
We are learning that Earth's tectonic plates move, creating geological features at plate boundaries, and that evidence supports the theory of plate tectonics.
We are learning that the rock cycle transforms rocks between sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic types over different timescales, and their properties reflect how they formed.
We are learning that the changing positions of Earth, the Sun and the Moon cause predictable cycles including seasons, eclipses and tides.
We are learning that simple machines — like levers, pulleys, wedges and screws — change the direction or size of forces to make work easier.
We are learning that balanced and unbalanced forces determine whether an object stays still, speeds up, slows down or changes direction, and force diagrams help us represent this.
We are learning that energy exists in different forms, can be transferred and transformed, and that we can analyse how efficiently energy moves through a system.
We are learning that household energy use can be measured through an energy audit and is affected by the appliances we choose, building design, season and climate.
We are learning that electrical circuits transfer energy when current flows, and they can be designed using different components for different purposes, described using voltage and current.
We are learning that scientific knowledge is validated and refined through methods such as replication, peer review, publication and building consensus — and it remains open to challenge.
We are learning that advances in technology enable advances in science, and that scientific discoveries in turn drive new technologies and engineering.

We are learning that using science to address real-world sustainability issues can produce diverse outcomes, and the extent to which society adopts scientific solutions depends on their projected impacts.
We are learning that scientific knowledge can be interpreted differently by different groups in society, and that societal values and needs can influence which research gets funded and pursued.
We are learning to formulate investigable questions, predictions and hypotheses that guide investigations aimed at testing and developing explanatory models.
We are learning to plan valid, reproducible investigations that control for sources of error and bias, manage risks, address ethical issues and follow cultural protocols on Country.
We are learning to select equipment, generate data with appropriate precision and consider sample size for reliable results, using digital tools where appropriate.
We are learning to organise, process and summarise data using tables, graphs, descriptive statistics, models, symbols, formulas and mathematical relationships.
We are learning to analyse and compare processed data to identify and explain qualitative and quantitative patterns, trends, relationships and anomalies.
We are learning to evaluate the validity and reproducibility of investigation methods and conclusions by identifying assumptions, biases, errors and areas of uncertainty.
We are learning to construct evidence-based arguments that support conclusions or evaluate claims, while considering ethical issues and cultural protocols for using secondary data.
We are learning to communicate and justify scientific ideas, findings and arguments by selecting appropriate formats, vocabulary, conventions and representations for diverse audiences.
We are learning that the structures of reproductive cells and organs in plants and animals are related to their functions, and that both sexual and asexual reproduction help species survive.
We are learning that DNA, chromosomes, genes and alleles work together in genetic inheritance, and that Mendelian principles can predict trait ratios in offspring.
We are learning that evolution by natural selection — involving variation, isolation and adaptation — explains both past and present biodiversity, and that all organisms are related to some degree.
We are learning that the atomic model evolved as electrons, protons and neutrons were discovered, and that natural radioactive decay transforms unstable atoms into stable ones.
We are learning that the periodic table organises elements by atomic structure, revealing patterns in properties such as reactivity, metallic character and atomic size across rows and groups.
We are learning that chemical reactions involve the rearrangement of atoms and are governed by the Law of Conservation of Mass, and that they can be represented by balanced equations.

We are learning that chemical reactions can be classified as synthesis, decomposition or displacement, and as exothermic or endothermic, and that factors like temperature and concentration affect reaction rates.
We are learning that carbon cycles through Earth's systems via processes like photosynthesis, respiration, combustion and volcanic activity, and that human actions affect this cycle.

We are learning that global climate change results from interactions between greenhouse gas emissions and energy exchanges within Earth's systems, and that mitigating it requires addressing multiple human activities.
We are learning that space exploration aims to expand our understanding of the universe's origins and structure, and to solve the challenges of humans living beyond Earth.
We are learning that the universe contains galaxies, stars, solar systems and black holes, and that the Big Bang theory — supported by evidence — models the origin and evolution of the universe.
We are learning that the nervous and endocrine systems work together to detect stimuli, coordinate responses and maintain a stable internal environment through feedback mechanisms.

We are learning that infectious diseases are caused by pathogens like bacteria, viruses and fungi, while non-infectious diseases have other causes, and that various measures can control disease transmission.
We are learning that wave and particle models describe how energy transfers through different media, and that waves have measurable properties like amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed.
We are learning that the Law of Conservation of Energy means energy in a system is never lost — only transferred or transformed — and we can measure how efficiently this happens.
We are learning that electricity can be generated as AC using magnets and turbines (powered by wind, water, steam or nuclear energy) or as DC using solar cells or batteries.
We are learning to use Newton's laws of motion to quantitatively analyse how force, mass and acceleration are related.
We learn to construct a main question and supporting sub-questions for different purposes.
We learn when and how to suspend judgement to support generating and evaluating ideas and possibilities.
We learn strategies for generating new ideas by identifying patterns across multiple information sources.
We learn to structure and communicate a conclusion and its justification where competing claims are analysed and evaluated.
We learn about reasons for competing claims on matters of fact and value, including the role of evidence and expertise.
We learn about more reasoning errors including cause-and-effect fallacies and arguing from ignorance, and how to improve reasoning when these errors occur.
We learn when and how to select criteria to support clear analysis and evaluation, including of competing claims.
We learn to select, use and reflect on both general and context-specific learning strategies.
We learn about the broad strengths and limitations of thinking processes in different contexts, including problem-solving.
We learn to develop criteria for evaluating proposed solutions and incorporate new knowledge that could affect our final decision.
We learn to analyse and improve the structure, clarity, consistency and coherence of a conclusion and its justification in different contexts.
We learn to analyse and evaluate claims for accuracy, precision, depth and breadth, and to identify when claims are used in misleading ways.
We learn about complex reasoning errors including false dichotomies and appeal to consensus, their significance and how to correct them.
We learn when and how to refine criteria to improve clarity and support analysis and evaluation, including of competing claims.
We learn ways to select, monitor and adapt general and context-specific learning strategies.
We learn the importance of critically analysing our thinking processes in different contexts, considering factors like cognitive biases.
We learn to develop and adapt criteria for evaluating the viability and sustainability of proposed solutions in different contexts.
We learn to construct and adapt questions to suit different contexts.
We learn when and how to critically reflect on suspending judgement when generating and evaluating ideas from different perspectives.
We learn strategies for generating new ideas including identifying links and patterns across multiple information sources and perspectives.
We learn the meaning of ethical concepts like justice, freedom, equality and non-maleficence and the criteria associated with them in different contexts.
We learn how ethical perspectives can be individual or shared, and why people develop similar or different ethical views based on their values and worldviews.
We learn how open-mindedness, personal and non-personal experiences, and context influence ethical perspectives and help explain their similarities and differences.
We learn how ethical perspectives and criteria are used to identify, explain and evaluate ethical issues and responses, including their significance.
We learn about the strengths and limitations of consequences, duties and virtues frameworks, and how these and alternative frameworks guide decision-making.
We learn how connections, distinctions and tensions between ethical concepts and perspectives are used to identify, analyse and respond to ethical issues.
We learn how multiple ethical frameworks can guide decision-making and explore similarities and differences between standard frameworks and alternatives.
We learn the distinction between ethical and legal, and the connections and tensions between ethical concepts like trust and integrity, or individual happiness and the common good.
We learn how and why ethical perspectives can be challenged and changed, including how cultural diversity challenges shared expectations, and what supports negotiating shared ethical views.
We learn how dispositions, experiences, emotions and context interconnect to influence and can challenge and change ethical perspectives.
We learn how cultures change over time and across contexts, and how this affects identity, belonging and inclusion.
We learn about attitudes, beliefs and behaviours that create cultural safety in different contexts.
We learn about the benefits and challenges of living and working in a culturally diverse society and an interconnected world.
We learn about the importance of rights and responsibilities and how they intersect with diverse worldviews in different contexts.
We learn the components of a cohesive, culturally diverse society and the benefits and challenges of building and maintaining social cohesion.
We learn how diverse worldviews can contribute to addressing social and environmental challenges.
We learn how diverse cultures influence one another and how this impacts identity, belonging and inclusion.
We learn how intercultural relations and experiences are influenced by the policies and practices of various institutions.
We are learning how people's values and beliefs shape who they are, how they can differ between people, and how those differences show up in relationships.
We are learning what human rights and responsibilities are, and how respecting them helps hold communities together and creates social cohesion.
We are learning about the factors that shape how we experience personal and group relationships — including boundaries, levels of closeness, power dynamics and social expectations.
We are learning to recognise when collaboration would be beneficial, how to set shared goals for our team, and practical ways team members can help each other succeed.
We are learning to recognise when our emotions are complex — when we feel multiple or conflicting things at once — and to understand what causes that complexity and how it affects us.
We are learning the difference between helpful and unhelpful coping strategies when facing challenges, and how to support our friends with empathy when they are going through difficult times.
We are learning when and how to use different skills and strategies to prevent, calm down and resolve conflicts — whether within our own group or between different groups.

We are learning strategies for reflecting on and developing our personal strengths so we can support ourselves and others, and how to connect our interests to broader life paths including potential careers.
We are learning strategies for building our confidence, adaptability and perseverance when facing challenges, including how to draw on our personal strengths and healthy coping methods.
We are learning what helps and what hinders us when it comes to working independently, making responsible decisions, and setting and achieving goals.
We are learning about the personal, social and cultural factors that shape our ability to have respectful relationships, and the rights and responsibilities that come with being in a relationship.
We are learning strategies for building and managing effective teams, and how to evaluate how well a team is collaborating and recommend improvements.
We are learning when and how to adapt our skills and strategies to prevent, calm down or resolve conflicts that happen within or between groups, across different contexts.

We are learning strategies for reflecting on, using and further developing our personal strengths to support ourselves and others in challenging situations, and how to connect our strengths and interests to planning for our future.

We are learning how to identify and adapt strategies for building confidence, adaptability and perseverance in response to challenges across different contexts, taking into account what helps and what gets in the way.
We are learning about the importance of taking individual responsibility and being adaptable when making decisions, completing challenging tasks and planning for what comes next in our lives.
We are learning how people's different values and beliefs lead to different perspectives on social issues, and exploring both the benefits and challenges that come from having diverse viewpoints.

We are learning what barriers and enablers exist for accepting diversity, how to evaluate strategies for being respectful, and how to navigate situations where different human rights and responsibilities may compete with each other.
We are learning how to analyse and evaluate emotional complexity — situations where we feel multiple or conflicting emotions — across different contexts and from different people's perspectives.

We are learning when and how to choose effective help-seeking and coping strategies for different situations, and how to provide meaningful peer support and empathetic communication when others need us.
We are learning about the role of political parties and independent representatives in Australian democracy, including how elections and referendums work.
We are learning about how well Australia's institutions and systems uphold democratic values like freedom of speech, religious freedom, and the right to a fair trial.
We are learning about the Australian Constitution and how key institutions and political actors interact to govern the country.
We are learning about how citizens stay informed about and participate in Australia's democracy, including through electoral and digital systems.

We are learning about how Australia's secular democracy and multi-faith society is shaped by diverse cultural origins, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, British-European, and broader global influences.
We are learning about how values based on freedom, respect, fairness, and equality of opportunity can support a cohesive, diverse society.
We are learning about how groups express their identities — including religious and cultural identity — and how this can both strengthen and challenge social cohesion.

We are learning about different experiences and perspectives on national identity and citizenship, including connections between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander identities and Australian national identity.
We are learning to develop and refine sharp questions that help us investigate current political, legal, and civic issues in depth.
We are learning to analyse contemporary issues by finding, selecting, explaining, and comparing information from different sources.
We are learning to explain how cultural, religious, and social influences have shaped Australia's democratic institutions.
We are learning to analyse how democratic values and legal principles are expressed through Australia's democratic institutions and processes.
We are learning to explain how political actors — like the Prime Minister, ministers, and opposition — exercise power within democratic institutions.
We are learning to participate in democratic decision-making processes like building consensus and voting.
We are learning to examine different methods of civic participation in issues at local, state, and national levels, and explain why and how people use them.
We are learning to develop a well-supported analysis of civic issues using knowledge, evidence, and multiple methods of communication.
We are learning about the key principles and features of the Australian legal system, including the Constitution, common law, and the presumption of innocence.
We are learning about how citizens can participate in and influence the process of making laws, including by contacting their elected representatives.
We are learning about the characteristics of laws in Australia and how they are made through parliaments (statutory law) and through courts (common law).
We are learning about the types of law in Australia — criminal and civil — and the place of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander customary law.
We are learning about the key features of Australia's court system — its structure, jurisdictions, and how courts and tribunals operate, including alternative dispute resolution methods.
We are learning about the role of parliaments and the High Court of Australia in protecting rights under the Constitution, including through landmark judicial decisions.
We are learning about how Australia's international legal obligations influence domestic lawmaking and government policies in areas like human rights and environmental protection.
We are learning to evaluate how well Australia's legal systems deliver justice, compared with at least one other country's approach.
We are learning about how individuals and groups participate in and contribute to civic life and global citizenship, including through environmental and human rights activism.
We are learning about the challenges to sustaining a resilient democracy and a cohesive society in Australia, and the strategies used to address them.
We are learning about the influence of various media — including social media — in shaping identity, attitudes, and perceptions of issues in society.
We are learning to develop and evaluate the quality of questions that guide our investigation of contemporary political, legal, and civic issues.
We are learning to evaluate information, data, perspectives, and ideas from a range of sources on contemporary civic issues.
We are learning to recommend changes to political, legal, or civic institutions and justify our recommendations with evidence and reasoning.
We are learning to evaluate how well the principles of justice — fairness, equality, and access — are achieved through Australia's democratic and legal institutions.
We are learning to evaluate the power of Australian and international political actors in relation to contemporary issues.
We are learning to evaluate the effectiveness of democratic decision-making processes and their outcomes.
We are learning to participate in civic processes and evaluate which methods and strategies of civic participation are most effective for different issues.
We are learning to construct sustained, evidence-based arguments about civic issues using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts, and disciplinary methods.

We are learning about the role of the Australian Constitution in establishing the federal system of government and democratic processes, including how the Constitution can be changed through referendums.
We are learning about the processes through which government policy is shaped, developed, and implemented — including the roles of political parties, interest groups, media, and the public service.

We are learning to compare the key features and values of Australia's system of government with at least one other system — examining similarities, differences, and how well each upholds democratic values.
We are learning about the Australian Government's roles and responsibilities at regional and global levels, including its involvement in the United Nations and international agreements.
We are learning about the fundamental economic problem of scarcity — that resources are limited while wants are unlimited — and how this forces us to make choices involving trade-offs.
We are learning about how a free market works — driven by supply and demand, and the idea that consumers' choices guide what is produced.
We are learning about the different purposes, goals, and types of businesses — including sole traders, partnerships, and companies — and the categories they fall into based on size and ownership.
We are learning about entrepreneurship and what makes it successful, including examples of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander entrepreneurship.
We are learning about why people work and the different ways Australians earn an income — through wages, salaries, investments, and other means.
We are learning about how the nature of work is changing in Australia and what predictions experts make about the future of work.
We are learning to develop and apply focused questions to investigate current issues related to economics, business, work, or finance.
We are learning to find, select, and organise relevant data and information from a range of sources for economic investigation.
We are learning to build, read, and draw conclusions from graphs, models, and text about economic patterns and trends.
We are learning to analyse and verify the sources of data and information we use in our economic investigations.
We are learning to analyse a response to an economic or business issue, identifying the potential costs and benefits involved.
We are learning to create and present clear descriptions and explanations using economics and business terminology, supported by evidence and data.
We are learning about the legal and ethical rights and responsibilities that Australian consumers and businesses have.
We are learning strategies to become a smart consumer, including how to identify and avoid financial scams.
We are learning about the Australian taxation system and how the revenue from taxes is used to fund public services.
We are learning about financial planning skills, including how to create a budget and set personal financial goals.
We are learning about changing patterns in Australia's international trade and the costs and benefits of globalisation for different groups.
We are learning about the strategies and tactics businesses use to create and maintain a competitive advantage in the marketplace.
We are learning about how businesses use human resource management to motivate employees, improve performance, and achieve their goals.
We are learning about the role of trade unions and employer groups in the workplace and how they advocate for the interests of their members.
We are learning about managing consumer and financial risks and rewards — including identifying scams, making smart investments, and managing debt responsibly.
We are learning about superannuation — what it is, who contributes, why it matters, and the potential benefits of starting early.
We are learning to develop and modify questions that are suitable for investigating contemporary economic, business, work, or financial issues and systems.
We are learning to find, select, organise, and analyse relevant information and data from a range of sources for economic investigation.
We are learning to evaluate and use data and information effectively to address economic, business, work, or financial issues.
We are learning to draw logical conclusions from data and information gathered from verified sources.
We are learning to develop and evaluate a response to an economic or business issue using cost-benefit analysis and other economic decision-making tools.
We are learning to evaluate sources of data and information to determine their authenticity and validity for economic investigations.
We are learning to explain and present persuasive arguments about economics and business concepts and issues, using subject-specific knowledge, terminology, and evidence.
We are learning about economic policy — including fiscal and monetary policy — and how the circular flow model explains the movement of money, goods, and services through the economy.
We are learning about how the government and the Reserve Bank of Australia intervene in the economy to improve economic performance and address issues like inflation and unemployment.
We are learning about economic indicators — like GDP, unemployment rate, inflation, and the trade balance — that measure economic performance and influence economic decisions.
We are learning that water is a renewable resource, the different forms it takes in the water cycle, and how water resources vary across time and place.
We are learning about the environmental, economic, cultural, spiritual, and aesthetic uses and value of water — including for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
We are learning about where Australia's water resources are located, how much they vary, and how climate change is predicted to affect them.
We are learning about what causes water scarcity, and the different approaches used to overcome it in Australia, West Asia, and North Africa.
We are learning about the causes, impacts, and responses to atmospheric or water-related hazards like cyclones, floods, or droughts.
We are learning about the environmental, economic, social, and other measures used to assess how liveable a place is.
We are learning about how access to services and facilities — like transport, healthcare, and education — affects people's views about how liveable their place is.
We are learning about how environmental quality — such as clean air, green spaces, and water quality — affects how liveable people feel a place is.
We are learning about how social connections and a sense of community identity influence people's perceptions of how liveable a place is.
We are learning to apply the geographical concepts of space, environment, and interconnection to evaluate the liveability of places.
We are learning about responses and initiatives that aim to make places more liveable at a local scale.
We are learning to develop focused geographical questions for investigating phenomena, issues, or challenges.
We are learning to collect, organise, and process information and data from primary and secondary sources, including fieldwork and digital tools.
We are learning to present information and data using maps that follow cartographic conventions, as well as graphs, tables, and other visual formats.
We are learning to interpret and analyse information and data to identify similarities, differences, and patterns and explain what they mean.
We are learning to consider ethical values and draw evidence-based conclusions from our evaluation of geographical information and data.
We are learning to identify a strategy for action on environmental, economic, or social issues, explain what needs to be done, and justify our recommendation.
We are learning to create and present well-structured explanations and responses using geographical knowledge, concepts, methods, and evidence from multiple sources.
We are learning about different types of landscapes, the landform features that make them distinctive, and where they are found in Australia and around the world.
We are learning about the spiritual, aesthetic, and cultural value that landscapes and landforms hold for people, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
We are learning about the geomorphological processes — like erosion, weathering, and deposition — that create and shape landforms, including through a study of a local landform.
We are learning about how human activities change landforms and how these changes can be managed, including through studying a local example.
We are learning about the causes, impacts, and responses to geomorphological hazards like landslides, earthquakes, or volcanic eruptions.
We are learning how the geographical concepts of interconnection and change can help us understand environmental phenomena.
We are learning about the causes and patterns of urbanisation in rapidly urbanising countries, and its environmental, economic, and social effects.
We are learning about patterns of international and internal migration in Australia and China or other countries, and the reasons people move.
We are learning to compare urban patterns in highly urbanised countries, including comparing Australia and the United States or another country.
We are learning about strategies and responses designed to improve the liveability and environmental sustainability of Australian cities.
We are learning how the geographical concepts of space, place, interconnection, change, and sustainability can help us understand processes that transform places and reshape environments.
We are learning about how changing transportation and digital technology affect people's lives and places, including the environmental consequences.
We are learning about the economic and demographic impacts of international trade in manufactured products on different places.
We are learning about the impacts of trade interconnections — including trade in embodied carbon — on the sustainability and character of places.
We are learning about how people's travel, recreational, and cultural choices affect places, and how these impacts are managed.
We are learning about how the interconnectedness of the world influences the spatial spread of global trends in music, food, fashion, and other cultural expressions.
We are learning about ways to measure human wellbeing in different places — and how these measurements reveal spatial variations in quality of life.
We are learning about the reasons for and implications of spatial differences in human wellbeing at local scales and between countries.
We are learning about the specific reasons for and implications of spatial differences in the wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples across Australia.
We are learning about the role and responses of international, national, and non-government organisations in addressing differences in human wellbeing.
We are learning to develop a range of sophisticated questions for geographical inquiry into phenomena, issues, or challenges.
We are learning to collect, process, and compare information and data from primary and secondary sources — including fieldwork and digital tools — with attention to ethical considerations.
We are learning to represent and analyse information and data using a range of formats — including complex graphs, maps created with GIS technology, and statistical analysis.
We are learning to interpret and evaluate information and data to make generalisations and predictions, analyse trends, and draw conclusions about geographical issues.
We are learning to consider ethical values and diverse perspectives when justifying our conclusions about geographical phenomena, issues, or challenges.
We are learning to justify our proposed responses and develop and evaluate strategies for addressing geographical issues using environmental, economic, or social criteria.
We are learning to explain and evaluate proposed actions, using geographical knowledge and concepts and appropriate terminology, to communicate in a range of formats.
We are learning about the distribution and characteristics of biomes — large-scale regions defined by their distinctive climates, vegetation, soils, and living things.
We are learning about the environmental, economic, and technological factors that influence how crops are produced in Australia and other parts of the world.
We are learning about the environmental, economic, and social sustainability of farming in Australia.
We are learning about the environmental, economic, and political constraints on the world's food supply — including the impacts of climate change.
We are learning about human-induced environmental changes and their impacts on the sustainability of places and the wellbeing of communities.
We are learning about geographical approaches to understanding the causes and consequences of a selected environmental issue.
We are learning about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' approaches to custodial responsibility and sustainable management of the environment.
We are learning about how people's different environmental worldviews — their beliefs and values about nature — influence their support for or opposition to environmental sustainability measures.
We are learning about geographical approaches to managing a selected environmental issue — including how environmental, economic, and social considerations interact.
We are learning about different theories and evidence about early human evolution, migration, and the establishment of the earliest societies, including in Australia.
We are learning about the development and features of early societies, including their technologies, agriculture, trade, spiritual practices, and forms of government.
We are learning about the different methods and sources of evidence that historians and archaeologists use to investigate early societies and human evolution.
We are learning about the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' knowledge and understanding of the continent, oceans, and sky — accumulated over more than 60,000 years.
We are learning about how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples responded to environmental processes and changes over the course of their deep history.
We are learning about the features and structures of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and how they demonstrated continuity and change over time.
We are learning about significant beliefs and values of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples that shaped — and continue to shape — their communities.
We are learning about the cultural protocols for maintaining and preserving Country and Place, ancestral remains, cultural artefacts, and knowledge.
We are learning about the changing evidence and interpretations that support the recognition of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples as the world's oldest continuous cultures.
We are learning about how the physical environment influenced the development of an ancient society — shaping its food production, settlement patterns, trade, and culture.
We are learning about how ancient societies were organised, the significant groups within them, their perspectives, and their roles in the wider community.
We are learning about the significant beliefs, values, places, and practices of an ancient society and how they showed continuity and change over time.
We are learning about significant events or turning points in an ancient society and how they contributed to both continuity and change.
We are learning about the causes and consequences of contacts and conflicts within societies and between them, and how these resulted in change or continuity.
We are learning about the role, contribution, and achievements of a significant individual or group that changed an ancient society.
We are learning about how the significance of an ancient society or individual has been interpreted over time, and what legacies they left behind.
We are learning to develop and use historical questions that guide our investigations and help us build well-structured arguments.
We are learning to sequence significant events, individuals, ideas, and developments chronologically to explain patterns of continuity and change.
We are learning to explain the features, content, and context of historical sources in detail.
We are learning to analyse how valuable sources are as evidence for investigating significance, continuity, and change.
We are learning to explain the perspectives, beliefs, values, and attitudes of people and groups in the past, supported by evidence from historical sources.
We are learning to analyse historical interpretations and debates — understanding how and why historians disagree.
We are learning to explain continuity and change across a historical period, identifying what changed, what stayed the same, and why.
We are learning to explain the causes and consequences of significant events, ideas, and developments, and how they contributed to turning points in history.
We are learning to analyse the significance of individuals, events, sites, developments, and cultural achievements in history.
We are learning to construct our own historical interpretations using appropriate concepts, terms, evidence, and conventions of historical writing.
We are learning about the patterns of continuity and change caused by significant events between 600 CE and 1750 CE, including the spread of empires, trade, and ideas.
We are learning about the features of the pre-modern world, including social structures, contact between different societies, and conflicts.
We are learning about significant social, cultural, economic, environmental, and political continuity and change in the way of life of people who lived in a medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about the causes and consequences of a significant event or turning point that contributed to continuity and change in a medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about the experiences and perspectives of rulers and ordinary people, and how power and authority interacted with resistance in a medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about the role, contribution, and achievements of a significant individual or group that drove change in a medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about how historical events, individuals, groups, or institutions from the medieval or early modern period have been interpreted over time, and what legacies they left.
We are learning about significant social, cultural, economic, environmental, and political continuities and changes in another medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about the causes and consequences of a significant event or turning point in a second medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about the experiences and perspectives of rulers and ordinary people in a second medieval or early modern society, and how power and resistance interacted.
We are learning about the role, contribution, and achievements of a significant individual or group that drove change in a second medieval or early modern society.
We are learning about how historical events, individuals, groups, or institutions from a second medieval or early modern society have been interpreted, and their legacies.
We are learning about the causes and consequences of the Industrial Revolution, the movement of peoples, and European imperialism — including the colonisation of Australia.
We are learning about significant ideas and developments — such as the Enlightenment, democratic revolutions, and scientific advances — and their impacts on society and politics.
We are learning about significant developments and events since 1945 that have contributed to global change — such as decolonisation, the Cold War, and the emergence of new nation-states.
We are learning about significant movements for social and political change since 1945 — such as civil rights, women's rights, anti-apartheid, and environmental movements.
We are learning about the significant events, individuals, and groups in Australia's women's movement, and how it affected women's lives and broader Australian society.

We are learning about the continuing efforts to create change in civil rights and freedoms in Australia — including for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, migrants, women, and other groups.

units.title: Depth Study: Society in the Age of Imperialism

contentDescriptions.description: We are learning about the key social, cultural, economic, and political features of a society during the 18th and 19th centuries.
We are learning about the causes and consequences of contact with other countries and/or experiences of colonisation and liberation in a studied society.
We are learning about the significant events and influencing ideas that contributed to continuity and change in a studied society.
We are learning about the experiences and perspectives of individuals, groups, and movements within the studied society and the roles they played.
We are learning about the continuities and changes in ways of life, living conditions, political institutions, and cultural expression in the studied society over time.
We are learning about how the studied society's history has been interpreted differently over time — the debates and contested narratives.

units.title: Rights & Freedoms: Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander Peoples

contentDescriptions.description: We are learning about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' experiences and perspectives of colonisation, dispossession, and the ongoing impacts on their communities.
We are learning about the significant events, campaigns, and movements through which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have fought for rights and freedoms.
We are learning about the experiences and perspectives of significant individuals and groups who contributed to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rights movement.
We are learning about the effectiveness of the methods and tactics used to achieve Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' rights and freedoms.
We are learning about the rights and freedoms that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have secured since 1945 — and those that remain contested or unrealised.
We are learning about different historical interpretations and debates about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' rights and freedoms.
We are learning about how historical perspectives change over time in relation to developments in technology, society, politics, and the economy.
We are learning about the origins and significance of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including Australia's role in its development and its ongoing influence.
We are learning about the causes and consequences of significant post-1945 world events, ideas, and developments — and how they contributed to change.
We are learning about the continuities and changes caused by a major global influence, development, or event after 1945 in the world and in Australia.
We are learning about the perspectives of people who experienced a major global influence, development, or event after 1945 — including diverse viewpoints and contested narratives.
We are learning about different historical interpretations and debates about the changes and legacies of a major global influence, development, or event after 1945.
We are learning to formulate, refine, and use sophisticated historical questions to inform and structure our investigations.
We are learning to sequence significant events, individuals, ideas, movements, and developments chronologically to explain patterns of continuity and change.
We are learning to analyse the purpose, features, content, and context of historical sources with sophistication and precision.
We are learning to evaluate the value of historical sources as evidence for interpreting significance, continuity, and change.
We are learning to analyse the perspectives, beliefs, values, and attitudes of people and groups in the past, based on evidence from historical sources.
We are learning to evaluate historical interpretations and debates — assessing the evidence, reasoning, and perspectives that underpin competing claims about the past.
We are learning to analyse continuity and change with sophistication — identifying patterns, explaining causes, and assessing the significance of what changed and what persisted.
We are learning to analyse both short-term and long-term causes and the intended and unintended consequences of significant events, ideas, and developments.
We are learning to evaluate the significance of individuals, groups, movements, events, developments, and ideas using explicit criteria and evidence.
We are learning to construct sustained historical interpretations and arguments using appropriate historical concepts, terms, knowledge, conventions, and evidence from sources.

We are learning about the deep knowledge and understandings of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples that shaped their way of life before colonisation — including their science, technology, and governance systems.
We are learning about the causes of the establishment of British colonies on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' Countries and Places.
We are learning about the significant events, ideas, people, groups, and movements that contributed to continuity and change in Australian colonial society.
We are learning about the experiences and perspectives of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, locally-born colonists, and migrants during the colonial and post-colonial periods.
We are learning about the continuities and changes — and their consequences — on ways of life, living conditions, political rights, and identity in Australian society.
We are learning about the different interpretations and debates among historians about Australian history between 1750 and 1914 — including the history wars and contested narratives.
We are learning about the causes of World War I and World War II.
We are learning about the reasons Australians — including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples — fought in the world wars, and the differing motives and experiences of those who served.
We are learning about the significant places where Australians fought during the world wars.
We are learning about the experiences and perspectives of those who fought or were deployed overseas — including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander service personnel, women, and nurses.
We are learning about the significant events and turning points of the world wars.
